slides.name: Separate roles or an integrated explanation?

params.text: WHAT THE QUESTION REQUIRES, AND WHAT NODES ADDS
Separate roles or an integrated explanation?
Describe the main components of the CPU: each one’s role.
Describe the function of the processor and main memory: each one’s function.
Nothing beyond the list: a precise list of roles is the full answer.
How the two work together over the buses: teaches connected understanding.
Each component’s role, and what it manages, stores or controls.
A separate outcome: the function of the buses in reading from and writing to memory.

As written, both questions ask for separate roles. The integrated explanation is a Nodes extension, linked to a syllabus outcome. Whether a Singapore exam requires it needs its question and marking criteria.

slides.notes:
Separate roles or an integrated explanation? Both Nodes tasks are written for Nodes.
The minimum each requires: UK, each component’s role; Singapore, each part’s function. A precise list is the full answer when the question asks for a list of roles; it is not a weak answer.
What Nodes adds: in Singapore, how the two work together over the buses, as teaching that builds connected understanding. It is linked to SEAB 7155 outcome 1.1.3 (the function of data and address buses in reading from and writing to memory), a separate outcome, and is not required by the question as written.
The specimen paper on file, 7155/01 Q2(a), asks for the purpose of main memory alone. Whether any Singapore exam requires the interaction has to be checked against the question and what its marking criteria require the statements to mean; the number of marks does not settle the SOLO level.
This is a hypothesis about these examples, not a finding, and says nothing about how students in either system revise or answer.

slides.name: The answer: UK

params.text: Describe the main components of the CPU.
Control unit: decodes instructions and sends control signals that coordinate the other parts.
ALU: performs arithmetic and logical operations.
Registers: tiny, fast stores inside the CPU; the PC holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched.
Cache: fast memory close to the processor, for frequently used data and instructions.
Clock: provides timing signals that keep the CPU's operations in step.
6 useful elements: a planning count, not marks. From the Nodes stage: https://the-teaching-model.vercel.app/framework/gcse-cs/2

slides.notes:
UK · GCSE, the worked example: Control unit: decodes instructions and sends control signals that coordinate the other parts.
ALU: performs arithmetic and logical operations.
Registers: tiny, fast stores inside the CPU; the PC holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched.
Cache: fast memory close to the processor, for frequently used data and instructions.
Clock: provides timing signals that keep the CPU's operations in step.
Elements: 1 Control unit: its purpose: decodes instructions and sends control signals that coordinate the other parts; 2 ALU: its purpose: performs arithmetic and logical operations; 3 Registers: what they are: tiny, fast stores inside the CPU; 4 The PC: what it holds: the PC holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched; 5 Cache: its purpose: fast memory close to the processor, for frequently used data and instructions; 6 Clock: its purpose: provides timing signals that keep the CPU's operations in step.

slides.name: Where each answer slips

params.text: The near-miss looks different in each system.

“ALU: the brain of the CPU.
Registers: store data.”

layers.name: A label, and words that fit

params.text: A label, and words that fit any memory: not each part’s exact job.
Ask: “What exactly does it hold or do? Say it without a label.”
That is secondary storage, and nothing joins the processor to memory.
Ask: “What exactly does it hold or do? Say it without a label.”

layers.name: Names one part only: no user

params.text: Names one part only: no users, hardware or data.
Ask: “How do the parts work together?”

slides.notes:
UK, the stable answer: Control unit: decodes instructions and sends control signals.
ALU: the brain of the CPU.
Registers: store data.
Cache: stores data.
Clock: controls the speed of the computer.
Only the control unit has its exact purpose. “Stores data” could be any memory, so it says nothing about registers or cache; the ALU as “the brain” is a label; and the clock sends timing signals, it does not “control the speed”.
Singapore, the stable answer: The processor fetches, decodes and executes instructions. Main memory stores files.
The processor is right, but “stores files” describes secondary storage: main memory holds the program and the data being worked on, and nothing joins the two.
China, the weak answer: It is a computer program.
Names one part only: no users, hardware or data.

slides.name: Taught linkage: the UK examiner reports

params.text: TAUGHT LINKAGE · FIRST RESULTS · UK EXAMINER REPORTS
The reports show what a full answer needed, not how to teach students to build one.
Labels the purpose of each answer element.
The second mark explained, question by question
Models decisions about selecting and connecting knowledge.
“Apply it to the scenario”: said, not shown
Provides practice with progressively less support.
21 GCSE computer science examiner reports, 2019 to 2025: AQA 8525 (5), OCR J277 (8), Pearson Edexcel 1CP2 (3), WJEC and Eduqas (5). Advice to teachers, written after marking.

slides.notes:
Question: what do the UK boards make explicit to teachers about building an answer?
21 GCSE computer science examiner reports, 2019 to 2025: AQA 8525 (5), OCR J277 (8), Pearson Edexcel 1CP2 (3), WJEC and Eduqas (5).
1. Labels the purpose of each answer element. Partly found (6 of 21 reports). Reports name the job of the second mark question by question: the expansion that gives the reason, or the further detail the describe command word requires. They do it after marking, for one question at a time, not as a routine students are taught to apply. For example: OCR J277/02, June 2024, Q4(b); Pearson 1CP2/01, 2025, Q1(b)(ii); AQA 8525/1, June 2023.
2. Models decisions about selecting and connecting knowledge. Partly found (16 of 21 reports). The most common advice: apply the point to the scenario, avoid generic or vague answers, use the specific term. It says what the answer must do, but not how to choose the knowledge or make the connection. For example: OCR J277/01, June 2024, Q2(b)(i); AQA 8525/2, June 2022; Pearson 1CP2/01, 2025.
3. Contrasts incomplete and complete responses. Found (12 of 21 reports). OCR and Pearson reproduce candidates' answers with the marks they earned and what was missing, and OCR sets what candidates who did well did against those who did less well. AQA and WJEC describe stronger and weaker answers in prose, without reproducing them. For example: OCR J277/01, June 2022, Q3(d), Exemplar 3; OCR J277/01, June 2025; Pearson 1CP2/01, 2025.
4. Provides practice with progressively less support. Not found in the sampled materials. Practice advice is about programming, attempting every question and past papers. Where scaffolding is mentioned it describes the exam question itself (Pearson's programming paper has none), not support to withdraw over time. For example: OCR J277/02, June 2022 to 2025; Pearson 1CP2/02, 2023 and 2025.
5. Checks independent use. Not found in the sampled materials. OCR says the paper may ask candidates to apply knowledge to unfamiliar contexts, so the exam is the only check described. No report describes checking, before the exam, whether students build an answer unaided. For example: OCR J277/02, June 2022 to 2025.
In the UK reports, answer-building is made visible after the event: what a full answer needed, and where answers fell short. What the reports leave to teachers is the teaching in between: modelling the choice and the connection, and withdrawing support until students build the answer alone. That is the gap Nodes is built for, and it is a finding about these reports, not about UK teaching.

slides.notes:
UK: AQA 8525 specification and command words; OCR J277 specification, version 3.1 (May 2026).
Singapore: SEAB O-Level Computing 7155 syllabus (2026). MOE's 2024 G3 Computing teaching and learning syllabus, which is indexed with sections on pedagogy and assessment, was not examined: its official link returned “not found” on 12 October 2026 and its cover restricts it to education officers. Singapore’s teaching guidance is therefore not yet reviewed.
China: Ministry of Education, high-school Information Technology curriculum standard (2017; the Ministry's 2020 notice changed only its preface). Read from a scan by OCR.
1. Labels the purpose of each answer element.
  UK: Related guidance only. OCR defines Explain as “a detailed account including reasons or causes”; AQA as “set out purposes or reasons”. OCR’s CPU guidance asks for each component’s role and what it manages, stores or controls. This specifies what to know and what the whole answer does, not the elements to put in it. (OCR J277 PDF p.8 (6), p.34–35 (32–33); AQA command words)
  Singapore: Related guidance only. Outcomes carry the relationship itself: the function of each component and the buses; firewalls enforce security by monitoring packets against configurable rules. That specifies the content of an answer, not the elements students should put in one. (SEAB 7155 PDF p.6, p.12)
  China: Not found in the sampled materials. Outcomes name the action (描述, 理解) and the level, not the parts of an answer. (Module 2 requirements, PDF p.25–27 (16–18))
2. Models decisions about selecting and connecting knowledge.
  UK: Related guidance only. AQA ties programming experience to students being able to “articulate how programs work” and argue that a program is correct: instructional intent, but no model of selecting and connecting knowledge in a written answer. (AQA 8525 PDF p.9 (9))
  Singapore: Not found in the sampled materials. The exam syllabus sets outcomes and the exam; it gives no teaching advice. (SEAB 7155)
  China: Related guidance only. Teaching tips ask teachers to analyse typical systems with students and guide them to sum up the components, and to combine teacher demonstration with practice. It models analysing a system, not writing an answer. (Module 2 teaching tips, PDF p.25–26 (16–17); PDF p.38 (29))
3. Contrasts incomplete and complete responses.
  UK: Not found in the sampled materials. Not in the specifications; the examiner reports do this. (AQA 8525; OCR J277)
  Singapore: Not found in the sampled materials. Not in the syllabus. (SEAB 7155)
  China: Partly found. Case 3, a written item (propose the functions of an English-learning app), groups possible answers by level with scoring guidance. It sets weaker and stronger answers side by side, but does not show an incomplete answer being repaired. (Case 3, PDF p.67–68 (58–59))
4. Provides practice with progressively less support.
  UK: Not found in the sampled materials. Practice advice is for programming (“as much opportunity as possible”), not written answers. (AQA 8525 PDF p.9 (9))
  Singapore: Not found in the sampled materials. Not in the syllabus. (SEAB 7155)
  China: Related guidance only. Imitate first, then explore: teachers analyse good work, then give half-finished work for students to complete independently. This is scaffolding for a practical module (3D design); its use for written answers is not established. (Module 5 teaching tips, PDF p.38–39 (29–30))
5. Checks independent use.
  UK: Not found in the sampled materials. The exam assesses performance (AO2: apply knowledge in context). Nothing checks whether students construct the answer once instructional support is withdrawn. (OCR J277 PDF p.36 (34))
  Singapore: Not found in the sampled materials. The exam assesses performance; nothing checks independence after support is withdrawn. (SEAB 7155 PDF p.3)
  China: Related guidance only. Process assessment by classroom observation and evaluation of students’ work, and students completing an information system alone or in groups. This assesses practical performance; it does not check independent written answers after support is withdrawn. (PDF p.26 (17), p.61 (52))

slides.name: What the documents show

params.text: Knowledge and relationships are specified. A full sequence for teaching the written answer was not found.
Command words that say what the whole answer does, and AQA ties programming to explaining how programs work.
The required relationship written into each outcome: firewalls enforce security by monitoring packets against rules.
Demonstration, half-made work and possible answers by level: for practical work and one written item.
The question for Nodes: Where is the process of constructing the required response made explicit to students?
A finding about the sampled documents, not teaching across the three systems. Textbooks and classroom materials come next.

slides.notes:
The sampled documents specify required knowledge and relationships, and provide some relevant teaching and assessment guidance: the UK’s command words, Singapore’s relationships written into outcomes, China’s demonstration, scaffolding and answers by level. This review has not identified a complete sequence that explicitly teaches written-answer construction and progressively withdraws support. That is a finding about the sampled documents, not teaching across the three systems.
Found: the document explicitly teaches constructing a written answer this way. Related guidance only: an adjacent practice (content guidance, practical scaffolding, assessment of performance), not the thing itself.
The question for Nodes: Where is the process of constructing the required response made explicit to students?
